analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax entirely.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill drew 102 cosponsors, 96 of them Republicans, but never got a vote and died in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal taxes on inherited wealth: the estate tax owed when someone dies, the gift tax on large lifetime transfers, and the tax on transfers that skip a generation. The federal estate tax only applies to the largest estates, since smaller estates fall under an exemption, so the direct benefit goes to heirs of the wealthiest families. The bill's own text says these taxes raised about 1% of federal revenue, so repeal would leave that money to be made up by other taxpayers or by more borrowing.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates would keep the biggest share of their inheritances. Owners of large family businesses and farms would avoid the need to sell assets to pay the tax, the problem the bill's findings section highlights. Estate planners, trust lawyers, and life insurers selling estate-liquidity products would lose a major sales pitch.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire federal transfer-tax system: estate taxes at death, gift taxes on large lifetime transfers, and the generation-skipping transfer tax, effective for deaths and transfers after enactment.
Eliminates a tax that, per the bill's own findings, can take 37% to 55% of a large estate's value at death, forcing some small business and farm owners to sell assets to pay the bill.
Per the bill's findings, these taxes raised only about 1% of federal revenue in fiscal 1994, so for the families that do owe them the rates are high relative to what they contribute to the Treasury.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall by roughly the 1% of receipts these taxes raise, made up through higher taxes on everyone else, spending cuts, or more federal borrowing. The benefit would flow overwhelmingly to a small number of the largest estates, since ordinary families' estates fall below the taxable threshold.

drawbacks.text: Repeal forgoes the federal government's most progressive tax. The estate tax applies only to estates above an exemption threshold, so its burden falls almost entirely on the wealthiest households; eliminating it shifts that 1% of revenue onto everyone else or onto future taxpayers through borrowing.
The bill contains no replacement revenue or offset, so the full cost of repeal would add to deficits or require other tax increases.
Even supporters would have to acknowledge that the direct savings go to a narrow group: families whose estates are large enough to owe the tax in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for repeal rests on real hardships: some heirs to farms and small businesses have had to sell assets to cover the tax, and estate planning to avoid it wastes real resources. But the bill is a blunt instrument for that problem. Rather than raising the exemption or easing the burden on family businesses, it eliminates the entire tax on the largest fortunes, giving its largest benefit to the very wealthiest estates while removing about 1% of federal revenue that everyone else would have to make up. A narrower fix for small farms and businesses would have captured much of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Cox introduced the bill on February 1, 1995, with 20 original cosponsors including House Majority Leader Dick Armey.
It gathered 102 cosponsors, 96 Republicans and 6 Democrats.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, and the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers who would have picked up the lost revenue came out ahead, along with the principle of taxing the largest inheritances. Heirs of very large estates and the estate-planning industry are worse off that it never passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; large heirs lost out

for.name: Christopher Cox
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

for.name: 102 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including House Majority Leader Dick Armey
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 96 Republicans and 6 Democrats, signaling broad House Republican support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 1, 1995 and never reported it out or scheduled action, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Of 102 cosponsors, 96 were Republicans and 6 were Democrats, and the original cosponsor list was almost entirely Republican; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.note: Repeal would let the largest estates pass wealth between generations without federal transfer tax, a benefit concentrated in the top sliver of families. The forgone revenue, roughly 1% of federal receipts, would be made up by everyone else.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and trust services
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the elaborate trusts and planning devices families buy to reduce estate tax exposure, removing a major line of business. That lost cost is a saving to affected families.

Owners of large family businesses and farms would no longer face forced asset sales to cover the tax, the hardship the bill's findings emphasize. The benefit only reaches those whose holdings are large enough to owe the tax.
A common use of life insurance is providing cash to pay estate taxes; repeal would shrink that market. Policies bought to protect family liquidity have some value independent of the tax.
